newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore gas oil seen steady despite futures fall.
newsitem.headline: Singapore gas oil seen steady despite futures fall.

text.p: Singapore gas oil is expected to consolidate around its five-year record high trade despite a hefty drop to prices in the west, traders said on Friday.
"Singapore has held very well and we expect prices to be supported by buying from China and Indonesia," a trader at an oil major said.
Traders said they also expected an upward correction in prices in the west.
"Prices in the west should rebound and correct as heating oil stocks in the U.S. are still low," one trader said.
"Despite the big falls on the IPE, Singapore gas oil prices continue to lag the west," one trader said.
On Thursday gas oil traded in Singapore at a five-year record of $30.00 per barrel on a free-on-board basis -- before the big falls in western markets.
Singapore prices are currently about $7 per tonne below IPE levels, much narrower than the record $20.50 seen earlier this month.
Because prices in Singapore are still below that of the west, no arbitrage cargoes are expected to head to this region, which should be another factor supporting Asian gas oil prices.
Traditionally, prices in the east have been higher than those in the west but this relationship changed this year following the start up of new refining capacity in Thailand and South Korea.
Traders said they expected African demand to be met from the Middle East rather than the more expensive Mediterrenean--their previous source.
This would mean spot Middle East exports to Asia would remain scarce, as was the case in September and October, one trader said.
In addition to the limit on supplies, regional demand is the other component that is expected to keep prices stable.
Big consumers in China and Indonesia have shown recently that when it came to the crunch they are able to pay the high international prices for their gas oil, one trader said.

China in recent days bought up to 100,000-tonnes for arrival in late October and early November at between $227 and $230 per tonne on a cost-and-freight basis. Traditionally, they have been reluctant buyers when delivered prices went above $210 per tonne.
"It's not clear if China will continue to buy at these levels or whether they are going to lower their bids sharply (due to the big drop on the IPE)," one trader said.

On top of this, sources said that barge lot business on an ex-terminal basis in Hong Kong was also brisk and oil majors there have imported more than 100,000-tonnes for arrival in October to meet this extra demand.

Traders said Indonesia has also raised its spot purchases due to the lower operating rate of its 200,000-barrel-per-day (bpd) Cilacap crude unit as the refinery struggles to restart a 55,000-bpd visbreaker after a scheduled maintenance.
